title: Replacing 12K LoC with a 200 LoC Skill — David Gomes, Cursor
talk_summary: Cursor replaced ~12-15K LoC of native worktree/best-of-N feature code with ~200 lines of markdown skills plus sub-agents, gaining maintainability and multi-repo support but losing hard isolation guarantees. The core lesson is that agent-facing orchestration logic can often live in prompts/skills instead of code, and that the main risk (agents escaping their sandbox) must be caught with evals and system reminders.

takeaways.technique: Replace orchestration code with markdown skills
takeaways.what_they_do: They reimplemented a complex feature (worktree creation, setup scripts, isolation, judging) as ~200 lines of markdown instructions loaded on demand, deleting ~15K LoC.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we recently replaced a lot of code in the cursor application with just markdown, just a skill
takeaways.numbers: ~15,000 LoC deleted; new skill ~200 LoC; best-of-N skill ~40 lines vs ~4,000 before

takeaways.technique: Parent agent spawns per-model sub-agents then judges
takeaways.what_they_do: A parent agent creates one sub-agent per model, each in its own worktree/context, waits for all, then compares and can stitch together the best parts.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we're instructing the parent agent to go and create sub agents for each model, and then spin up a work tree for each

takeaways.technique: Two-scorer headless-CLI eval for sandbox adherence
takeaways.what_they_do: They run the headless Cursor CLI and score with two checks: did the agent work in its worktree, and did it wrongly touch the primary checkout.
takeaways.evidence_quote: One that checks to see if the model did any work in its work tree as expected, and then another one, which is the reverse of that

takeaways.technique: Per-model capability differences surfaced by evals
takeaways.what_they_do: Evals showed smaller models (Haiku) frequently deviate from instructions while stronger ones (Composer, Grok) stay on track, informing which model to use where.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Haiku, which is a smaller, less intelligent model, will very often deviate and start working in the primary checkout

takeaways.technique: System reminders to keep agent on track
takeaways.what_they_do: They inject periodic system reminders reinforcing the constraint (stay in this worktree) because models forget over long sessions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: another thing we can do is have better system reminders to the models uh instructing them to stay on track

takeaways.technique: Prompt-level isolation is weaker than hard isolation
takeaways.what_they_do: They admit the skill-based approach trusts the model ('vibes-based') versus the old code that made escaping physically impossible, and are partially reverting to native enforcement.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Now, we're trusting the model. So, it's you could say it's a bit vibes-based
